title: Chemistry of transition elements
overview: Understand transition metal complexes and ligands, the origin of colour, and their role as catalysts. This guide turns the current syllabus outcomes into a connected revision sequence: learn the ideas, practise the method, then use the recall cards and checklist to diagnose what still needs work.
syllabusPoints: Identify transition elements and write d-block ion electron configurations.
Describe complexes, ligands, coordination numbers, shapes and ligand exchange.
Explain colour and variable oxidation states, and use E° data for redox chemistry.
Explain transition-metal catalysis and use stability constants qualitatively/quantitatively.

definitions.definition: A d-block element forming at least one stable ion with an incomplete d subshell.
An ion or molecule donating a lone pair to a central metal ion.
A central metal ion bonded to surrounding ligands by coordinate bonds.
The number of coordinate bonds to the central metal ion.
Replacement of one ligand in a complex by another.
An equilibrium constant for formation of a complex from a metal ion and ligands.
Separation of d-orbital energy levels by the ligand environment.

sections.title: Electronic structure and oxidation states
content: Remove 4s electrons before 3d when forming first-row transition-metal ions. Variable oxidation states arise because 3d and 4s energies are similar. Use oxidation numbers, charge and ligand charges to identify the metal state.
bullets: Zn is d-block but Zn²⁺ is d¹⁰, so it does not meet every characteristic transition definition.
State electron configurations for the ion, not only the atom.

sections.title: Complexes and ligand exchange
content: Common ligands include H₂O, NH₃, Cl⁻, CN⁻ and bidentate ethanedioate/ethane-1,2-diamine. Coordination 6 is usually octahedral; coordination 4 may be tetrahedral or square planar. Ligand exchange changes colour, charge and sometimes geometry.
bullets: Count donor atoms, not ligand molecules, for coordination number.
Write balanced ionic equations for exchange.

sections.title: Colour, redox and stability
content: Ligands split d orbitals; visible light promotes a d electron and the complementary colour is observed. d⁰ and d¹⁰ ions usually lack d–d colour. Use E° values to judge redox direction. Large Kstab favours complex formation; chelating ligands often gain stability partly through entropy.
bullets: Colour depends on metal, oxidation state, ligand and geometry.
E° predicts feasibility, not reaction rate.

sections.title: Catalysis
content: Homogeneous transition-metal catalysts use variable oxidation states and form intermediates, providing a lower-energy sequence. Heterogeneous metals provide adsorption sites; reactant bonds weaken, surface reaction occurs and products desorb, freeing sites.
bullets: A catalyst is regenerated by the end of the mechanism.
Explain poisoning as blocking active sites where relevant.

diagram.title: Chemistry of transition elements: revision route

examTips: When naming or describing a complex, determine metal oxidation state, ligand count and overall charge separately.
Use equations plus visible observations in ligand-exchange answers.
Use precise chemical vocabulary, balanced equations and stated conditions; link every observation or trend to particles, bonding or equilibrium.
commonMistakes: Equating number of ligand molecules with coordination number for bidentate ligands.
Saying the catalyst changes the equilibrium constant.

quickRecall.question: Which electrons are removed first from a first-row d-block atom?
What does coordination number count?
quickRecall.answer: Coordinate bonds/donor atoms attached to the central ion.

quickRecall.question: Why are many transition-metal complexes coloured?
quickRecall.answer: Visible light is absorbed to promote electrons between ligand-split d levels.

quickRecall.question: Why can transition metals catalyse redox reactions?
quickRecall.answer: They access multiple oxidation states and form intermediates, creating lower-energy pathways.
